explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF sends row-count messages for statements in the procedure, adding client and network overhead.
With XACT_ABORT OFF, some runtime errors can leave an explicit transaction open after a statement fails.
@CustomerIdText embeds customer ID 1 rather than using the caller's customer selection.
@OrderID starts as the fixed business key 1, which the first OrderID filter uses instead of a caller-supplied key.
SELECT * returns every Orders column, including large text fields, and makes the result shape depend on the table schema.
TOP (10) does not specify which ten orders to return.
Orders.OrderID is the primary key, so DISTINCT cannot remove any duplicates from this result.
NOLOCK allows the Orders query to read uncommitted data and can produce missing or duplicate rows during concurrent writes.
YEAR wraps OrderDate, preventing the predicate from expressing a direct range on the date column.
The OrderDate filter fixes the reporting year at 2016 rather than taking it as input.
Orders.CustomerID is int, so SQL Server implicitly converts the nvarchar variable @CustomerIdText to int before comparing it.
The OR combines an unfiltered scan case with a CustomerID lookup, making it harder to choose one efficient plan for both.
The leading wildcard in the Comments pattern prevents a prefix-based index seek.
The Comments filter embeds the search term 'urgent' rather than accepting a search term as input.
ISNULL wraps the indexed CustomerID in the predicate even though the column is declared NOT NULL.
The predicate selects customer ID 1 directly instead of using a customer parameter.
Adding zero to OrderID has no effect on the value and obscures a direct equality predicate on the primary key.
CustomerID <> 1 can match most of Orders, making the CustomerID index less useful for this filter.
The excluded customer ID is fixed at 1 without a named business rule or input.
The CROSS JOIN pairs orders with unrelated customers because it does not match them on CustomerID.
TOP (1) picks an arbitrary order and customer pair from the cross join.
The comma join separates the Orders-OrderLines relationship from the table list, making the join condition easier to miss.
TOP (1) picks an arbitrary row from the Orders-OrderLines join.
The line-count subquery depends on each outer OrderID and can require repeated access to OrderLines instead of grouping the lines once.
The EXISTS check depends on each outer OrderID. Joining to a set of distinct qualifying OrderIDs would preserve one result per order.
The qualifying line quantity threshold is fixed at 1 without a named rule or parameter.
ORDER BY repeats the CASE expression for HasComments instead of referencing the alias, so the two expressions can drift apart.
ORDER BY 2 depends on the position of OrderDate and can silently change meaning if the select list is reordered.
OrderDate is not unique, so tied orders can move between pages. OrderID would provide a stable tie-breaker.
The two branches select different OrderID values, so UNION performs duplicate elimination that UNION ALL would avoid.
The first UNION branch embeds order ID 1 rather than accepting an order key as input.
The second UNION branch embeds order ID 2 rather than accepting an order key as input.
The predicate asks for a count of matching OrderLines even though it only needs to know whether one exists.
The assignment can read multiple Orders rows and leaves @OrderID with whichever value is processed last, without a defined order.
The insert into @OrderIds does not specify which five order keys to retain.
SELECT INTO infers the schema of #ImplicitOrders from the query rather than declaring the temporary table explicitly.
The query populating #ImplicitOrders does not specify which five orders to retain.
The cursor query does not specify which two orders to select or which order the first fetch will return.
The statement converts @CustomerID to text and concatenates it into executable SQL rather than binding it as an integer.
EXEC runs the customer lookup as text without binding its CustomerID filter, so different values can produce separate cached plans.
The statement converts @OrderID to text and concatenates it into the lookup rather than keeping the SQL text constant.
The call to sys.sp_executesql supplies no parameter definition or binding for the OrderID filter.
#Scratch is explicitly created but never dropped, so it remains in scope until the procedure exits.
The CATCH block returns the error message in a result set without rethrowing or returning a failure status.
The negative-order-ID check uses RAISERROR rather than THROW; RAISERROR does not honor XACT_ABORT.
PRINT emits a buffered, unstructured diagnostic that clients may not receive promptly.
The lookup embeds customer ID 1 instead of using the existing customer parameter.
The Orders query embeds a January 1, 2016 cutoff without naming it or exposing it as an input.
CONVERT has no explicit style for '01/02/2016', so session settings can make it mean January 2 or February 1.
TOP (1) does not specify which matching order to return from the invoice join.
COALESCE unnecessarily wraps Orders.CustomerID, which is NOT NULL, instead of comparing the join key directly.
COALESCE unnecessarily wraps Invoices.CustomerID, which is also NOT NULL, instead of comparing the join key directly.
TOP (1) returns an arbitrary order because the query does not define an ordering.
Joining Orders to itself on its primary key matches each order to the same row and supplies no additional data.
Sorting all orders by the nvarchar(max) Comments column can require substantial sort memory and spill to tempdb.
The quantity total must process all rows in Sales.OrderLines because there is no filter.
OrderID > 0 is a row-level predicate on the grouping key and can be applied in WHERE before grouping.
The unfiltered COUNT(*) must count every row in Sales.Orders.
COUNT(*) without GROUP BY returns a single row, so ordering by OrderCount has no effect.
MERGE adds concurrency and correctness hazards even though this code only needs an update for a matched OrderID.
The matched MERGE action assigns Comments to itself and can still incur write overhead or fire update triggers.
SET Comments = Comments leaves the stored value unchanged but can still take write locks or fire update triggers.
Deleting by Quantity alone can remove matching lines across unrelated orders rather than targeting a specific order line.
The delete uses -1 as a special quantity without naming or documenting what that value represents.
WAITFOR DELAY holds the request open for one second without doing database work.
The transaction starts outside TRY/CATCH, leaving no local error handler to ensure rollback on failure.
IDENTITY_INSERT is enabled for Sales.Orders even though the block does not insert an identity value.
The sp_who call omits the sys schema qualifier.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is not reset within the procedure, so later queries and writes can stop after one row.
The VALUES insert into #DemoCategories depends on column order rather than explicitly naming CategoryID and CategoryName.
The new category is always assigned the fixed CategoryID 99.
Prepending '%' makes the CustomerName search a substring match and prevents a prefix seek on the name index.
Caller-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated directly into executable SQL, allowing the input to alter the statement. Bind the search value as a parameter.
The sp_executesql call supplies no bindings, so changes to the search value change the SQL text and reduce plan reuse.
The sp_executesql call omits the sys schema qualifier.
The update does not identify a target customer. The active ROWCOUNT limit can cap the write, but it does not determine which customer is updated.
The update assigns CustomerCategoryID 1 rather than accepting the desired category as input.
The WHERE condition on o.OrderDate rejects NULL-extended rows, excluding customers with no qualifying order despite the LEFT JOIN.
The order-date filter embeds a January 1, 2016 cutoff instead of naming it or accepting it as input.
DeliveryMethodID = NULL does not evaluate to true under ANSI NULL semantics, so this filter returns no customers.
dbo.GetCustomerType can execute separately for each customer row if SQL Server cannot inline the function.
The handler returns ERROR_MESSAGE() as data but does not signal that the transactional delete failed.
The handler does not check or roll back the transaction started in TRY, so a failure can leave it open or uncommittable.
INDEX = 1 forces a specific Customers index and prevents the optimizer from choosing a more suitable access path.
Three nested derived tables only pass CustomerID through; a single query would express the same filter without the extra nesting.
The '%A%' pattern starts with a wildcard, preventing a prefix seek on the CustomerName index.
The CustomerName filter fixes the search term at 'A' rather than accepting a search value as input.
SELECT * makes the result depend on every column returned by dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti.

The function definition is not supplied. If dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement TVF that can be expressed as one query, an inline TVF would give the optimizer more visibility into its result.
